newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU plans to clear ship aid in Germany, Spain, Greece.
newsitem.headline: EU plans to clear ship aid in Germany, Spain, Greece.

text.p: The European Commission, disappointed by a U.S. delay in ratifying a deal to cut support for the shipbuilding industry, on Wednesday proposed approving aid to German, Spanish and Greek shipyards.

The EU executive had delayed a decision on the three countries' request to grant the aid, preferring to wait for U.S. ratification of the deal struck through the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
But the Commission decided to go ahead with its proposal to EU industry ministers after a meeting of the OECD, the club of wealthy industrial nations, failed to produce an outcome last week.
However, it tried to ease concerns among other shipbuilders, saying the restructuring aid would not significantly boost the yards' competitive position.
Governments involved had also undertaken not to pay any more rescue or restructuring aid to the shipyards in the future, the Commission said in a statement.
"In addition the Commission is insisting on important reduction in production capacity in Germany and Spain," it said. There would be strict monitoring of the conditions imposed on the shipyards.
The German aid would help two shipyards in former east Germany previously owned by bankrupt Bremer Vulkan.
The problems of MTW-Schiffswerft and Volkswerft Stralsund arose from alleged misuse by Bremer Vulkan of 850 million marks ($505 million) in subsidies intended for them.

"For the continuation and completion of the restructuring programmes new aid in the range of one billion marks is needed," the statement said. Of this, 728 million marks would need the approval of EU industry ministers.

In Greece, the proposal would allow Athens to write off 54.5 billion drachmas ($205 million) in debts accumulated by Hellenic shipyards before it was privatised in 1995. The Spanish support was needed for restructuring public yards to return them to viability by the end of 1998.

A large part of the proposed aid, 180 billion pesetas ($1.26 billion), was provided for in an exemption for Spain under the OECD deal. But a further 135 billion pesetas in interest payments, tax credits and capital injection were also needed.
Willy Helin, spokesman for EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, said there was a good chance the industry ministers would approve the proposal. They meet on April 24.
However, Britain and the Nordic EU countries are traditionally sceptical about state aid. "I can imagine there will be some member states who will not be too happy with it," an EU source said.

The proposed aid would have been allowed under the OECD agreement, EU officials said. But due to the lack of any positive outcome at the OECD meeting in Paris, the commission felt "obliged to act if the future of the yards concerned is not to be jeopardised".
"The Americans disappointed us because they asked for more time," Helin told reporters, adding that the United States might continue to give aid to its shipyards.
The United States is the only country which has not yet ratified the 1994 accord within the 29-nation OECD to slash the amount of aid which may be given to shipyards.
Among other things, U.S. shipyards argue they have not had enough time to adjust to the commercial era after the loss of military contracts at the end of the Cold War.
The OECD deal would end direct shipbuilding subsidies except social aid, and research and development aid.
The Spanish, German and Greek cases were restructurings that were underway and which had been discussed within the context of the OECD deal, the Commission said.
At the Paris meeting, the United States said it would put forward legislation which might lead to ratification.
"But there is nothing firm or final in that," said Peter Guilford, Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan's spokesman.
($1 = 265 drachmas)
($1 = 142.5 pesetas)
